idiom_name: host job queue / event loop (queueMicrotask, setTimeout, message events)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no user-visible queue class because the runtime is built around one: the agent keeps a job queue (the event loop), every callback is a queued job, and queueMicrotask/setTimeout/postMessage decide which queue you post to - microtasks drain before the next task and each job runs to completion. What replaces the classic structure is the host: a sender calls an async API and the callback runs later on the same thread, with run-to-completion freeing handlers from lock questions. An explicit array queue remains justified when you own the drain point and want per-frame batching or coalescing rather than letting the runtime interleave jobs.
pitfalls: Jobs are never preempted: a long drain blocks rendering and input, so cap the work per frame or split it across ticks.
Microtasks (queueMicrotask, promise jobs) drain before the next task and can starve the event loop entirely if they keep rescheduling themselves.
A plain array queue hands out live object references - mutating a payload after posting leaks newer state into older events, while postMessage/structuredClone would have copied it.
